The end nodes A and F have the maximum eccentricity 4 and are drawn in the accent color. The card returns their node ids, 1 and 6." width="100%"} The eccentricity of a node is the largest hop distance from it to any node it can reach. Periphery nodes are those whose eccentricity equals the maximum over the graph (the diameter), so they are the nodes farthest from the graph's center. Distances are computed by breadth-first search, so edge weights are ignored. The periphery is useful for: - finding the "outskirts" of a network, such as remote stations or fringe members - picking the endpoints of a longest shortest path (a diameter path) - checking how far the edges of a network sit from its core On a directed graph, distances follow edge direction, so a node's eccentricity only considers nodes it can reach. On a disconnected graph, each node's eccentricity is measured within its own component, and the periphery is the set of nodes whose eccentricity equals the largest value found in any component. The method does not modify the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs in the periphery, in no particular order. Empty for an empty graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The periphery is the set of nodes attaining the graph's diameter, that is those with $\mathrm{ecc}(v) = \max_u \mathrm{ecc}(u)$. It is the natural dual of the graph's *center* (minimum-eccentricity nodes) and reveals which parts of the network sit furthest from everything else. On a tree it always consists of leaves. Multiple nodes commonly tie for maximum eccentricity; all such nodes are returned. Computing every eccentricity takes one BFS per node, so the cost is $O(V \cdot (V + E))$. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a path graph `1-2-3-4-5`, the two endpoints are farthest from the graph's center, so they form the periphery: ::: {#20f9b7c3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(5) sorted(graph.periphery()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [1, 5] ``` ::: ::: In a tree, the periphery consists of the leaves at the ends of the longest paths. Here the long branch `D - E` makes `E` peripheral, along with the leaves `B` and `C` on the other side of the root: ::: {#25866a00 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("D", "E")]) ) sorted(graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.periphery()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['B', 'C', 'E'] ``` ::: ::: On a disconnected graph, eccentricity is measured within each component. A 5-node path alongside a separate 2-node path yields the ends of the longer path, whose within-component eccentricity (`4`) is the largest: ::: {#f1a6d5f1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(5) graph.add_path_graph(2) sorted(graph.periphery()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [1, 5] ``` ::: :::
